newsitem.title: JAPAN: Even as dollar rallies, Japan central bank silent.
newsitem.headline: Even as dollar rallies, Japan central bank silent.

text.p: Japan's central bank was mysteriously silent on Monday even as the dollar staged another unwelcome surge against the yen after the weekend meeting of the Group of Seven industrial nations, senior traders said.
The market believes the BOJ is ready to fight a rise in the dollar with massive selling in the open market.
But even as the dollar rose over 127 yen, there were no signs of market intervention or any of the usual signals the central bank gives that it might be coming.

"The BOJ (Bank of Japan) maintained utter silence despite the dollar soaring in the post-G7 market. But it may still be saving its energy for (dollar selling) intervention and the market is fully aware of that," said Takashi Okura, chief dealer at First National Bank of Chicago.
The dollar rose nearly one yen to 127.10 yen in morning trading and set a three-year high of 1.7395 German marks in Tokyo trading.
The dollar rally came after a surprisingly weak communique from the G7 nations on foreign exchange levels.
The final statement said "We emphasised the importance of avoiding exchange rates that could lead to the reemergence of large external imbalances."
The statement seemed to reflect concern among G7 members that a continued rise of the dollar, particularly against the yen, could lead to trade problems down the road.

But traders started buying dollars because the statement did not directly refer to any excessive weakness in the yen and contained no mention of the G7 nations acting in concert to address yen weakness any time soon.
Bank of England Governor Eddie George said on Sunday that G7 officials did not feel that the current dollar/yen exchange rate was creating imbalances.
He added that the exchange rate environment was in pretty good shape and that no one at the meeting expressed the need for an action plan to deal with any future currency moves.

Ichiro Ikeda, director of the foreign exchange department at Credit Suisse First Boston, said: "The G7 statement was just a warning signalling that Japan will act if the dollar rises sharply by one or two yen a day.
"There will be a clash between (the Japanese authorities) and the market if the dollar embarks on another strong rally."
"We assume that the BOJ will step in to sell dollars before it rises to 130 yen," said Noriyuki Takano, assistant director of foreign exchange sales at Barclays Bank Plc.
But some dealers remain sceptical of intervention as long as the dollar creeps up gradually.
"The BOJ officials (who are in charge of foreign exchange) showed displeasure about the dollar's rise in the early morning, but they are sitting on their hands," said a bank dealer.

A senior trader at a major Japanese bank said it may be difficult for Japan and the United States to lower the value of the dollar sharply amid jitters in U.S. financial markets, where another U.S. interest rate rise is anticipated in May.
"It would be inconsistent to push the dollar down when the United States is trying to obviate inflationary fears and keep the economy from overheating," said the trader.
A strong dollar would help keep inflation in check and bring down U.S. long-term interest rates.
Despite lingering concerns about BOJ intervention, many traders said the dollar would cautiously test 130 yen.

Wataru Ito, deputy general manager at Sanwa Bank Ltd's treasury department, said: "There are no good reasons for selling dollars and buying yen, given higher U.S. interest rates and lingering worries about Japan's financial system."

Such worries were highlighted by Friday's collapse of medium-sized life insurer Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co, the latest in a series of financial failures since 1995, when Japan suffered its first bank failure of the postwar period.
